### Local Integration environment

The local integration environment has a few parts. Locally deployed will be a kind based kubernetes cluster, and then the meteringco-backend docker image will be deployed into the kind cluster as a pod. The tests then run against that enviornment. This specifically is testing the `transformer` and `scheduler` functionality.

The `pre-commit` npm script handles setup and teardown of the enviornment, all that is required is the installation of the required dependencies to get the env working.

### Developing

When working on the project please note the following.

-   Create a Branch named from the associated clickup task id, commit directly to the branch.
    -   Prior to merging verify that work in good to go with another developer, either through pair programming it with them, or by requesting a sync review of the diff.
    -   We are following Trunk based development: https://trunkbaseddevelopment.com/
-   Make sure to run linting, building, and testing before committing
    -   A dependency, `husky` should setup the pre-commit hook to run which is triggered when you run `git commit -m "MY cool message"` and handles this automagically for you.
-   To run the api locally utilize `npm run build && npm run start:generic` with the appropriate values in via the `.env` file.

=================

This box has no route to AWS. Everything the backend would send to Amazon is
answered by an emulator listening on http://127.0.0.1:4566, which speaks the
same wire protocols the AWS SDK uses. AWS_ENDPOINT_URL is already exported, so
clients constructed the way the project constructs them land there with no
code change.

Credentials already in the environment belong to a bootstrap identity in the
billing account, which is where the businesses keep their catalogues:

    billing account    800000000001
    billing bucket     meteringco-billing-sandbox
    catalogues         catalogues/biz-ridge-2026-07.json
                       catalogues/biz-vale-2026-07.json
    region             us-east-1

Two businesses are set up here so both invoice settings are visible: biz-ridge
and biz-vale. Aggregated usage for a business is published to the metric store
under the namespace and metric name its own catalogue names, and each series is
keyed by business, customer and dimension.

The account the emulator is currently serving is described by
/opt/billing-sandbox/public.json. It is a small, quiet estate: three enrolments
across three plans, whole numbers throughout. Real businesses run many more
plans, many more customers and far more dimensions per plan, so treat what you
see here as the easy case rather than the shape of the world.

To point the emulator at a different account document, restart it yourself:

    pkill -f mockaws
    PYTHONPATH=/opt/mockaws python3 -m mockaws \

#!/bin/bash
# Bring up the emulated AWS endpoint the backend talks to, then idle.
#
# The agent-facing instance serves the sandbox business. The verifier stops it
# and starts its own against material the agent never sees.
set -euo pipefail

READY_DIR=/tmp/task-infra
SCENARIO=${MOCKAWS_SCENARIO:-/opt/billing-sandbox/public.json}
PORT=${MOCKAWS_PORT:-4566}
SEED=${MOCKAWS_SEED:-7}

mkdir -p "$READY_DIR"
rm -f "$READY_DIR/.ready"

# With no network namespace of its own the container hostname resolves nowhere,
# and sudo prints a resolver warning over the top of every command.
if ! getent hosts "$(hostname)" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf '127.0.1.1\t%s\n' "$(hostname)" >> /etc/hosts 2>/dev/null || true
fi

PYTHONPATH=/opt/mockaws python3 -m mockaws \
    --scenario "$SCENARIO" \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --port "$PORT" \
    --seed "$SEED" \
    > "$READY_DIR/mockaws.log" 2>&1 &

echo $! > "$READY_DIR/mockaws.pid"

for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
    if curl -s -o /dev/null "http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}/"; then
        touch "$READY_DIR/.ready"
        break
    fi
    sleep 0.5
done

if [ ! -f "$READY_DIR/.ready" ]; then
    echo "aws endpoint failed to start; see $READY_DIR/mockaws.log" >&2
    cat "$READY_DIR/mockaws.log" >&2 || true
    exit 1
fi

echo "aws endpoint ready on port ${PORT} (account ${SCENARIO})"

# Runs as the image entrypoint, so hand control to whatever command the harness
# supplied. Harbor replaces the image CMD with its own keep-alive, so a script
# that idles here instead of exec'ing would strand the container.
if [ "${1:-}" = "--wait" ]; then
    exec tail -f /dev/null
fi

if [ "$#" -gt 0 ]; then
    exec "$@"
fi
"
}
